column1: What is the theological distinction between redemptio objectiva and redemptio subjectiva according to Goyret and Ad Gentes 2–3?
column2:
1. Redemptio objectiva: The objective reconciliation accomplished once and for all (semel et pro semper / ephapax) by Christ on Calvary for the entire human race.
2. Redemptio subjectiva: The personal, historical application and appropriation of that redemption to individual human beings across time and space through the Church and sacraments.

column1: Why does the "incarnational logic" (caro cardo salutis) require an ordained apostolic ministry rather than purely interior, private grace (CCC 875)?
column2: Because the Word took true human flesh, God chooses to save human beings through human beings within a visible, historical community. No one can mandate, baptise, or absolve oneself: grace is an objective gift received ab alio (from Another) through visible ministers empowered by Christ.

column1: What is the fundamental difference between a true mediator (or sacramental instrument) and an intermediary (intermedio)?
column2:
1. Intermediary: A third party who interposes himself between two extremes as a separating screen or for personal profit.
2. Mediator / Sacramental Instrument: Christ is the only Mediator; the ordained minister is not a barrier or third party, but an instrumental cause (causa instrumentalis) through whom Christ Himself acts in persona Christi Capitis. The bridge is the destination.

column1: What twofold purpose did Christ specify in Mark 3:13–15 when calling the Twelve ("ut essent cum illo" and "ut mitteret eos praedicare")?
column2:
1. Ut essent cum illo ("to be with Him"): Communion and future consecration (ontological belonging to Christ).
2. Ut mitteret eos praedicare ("to send them to preach"): Mission and participation in the sacra potestas (casting out demons, healing, preaching).

column1: What does the symbolic number Twelve signify regarding the transition from the Old Covenant priesthood to the New Covenant (Lumen Gentium 19)?
column2:
1. It represents the Twelve Tribes of Israel, establishing the Apostles as the foundation of the New Israel.
2. It definitively breaks with the hereditary Levitical caste (limited to the biological lineage of Aaron), opening the priesthood to a universal election from all peoples.

column1: Why does Catholic theology reject reducing the institution of Holy Orders exclusively to Christ's words at the Last Supper ("Hoc facite in meam commemorationem")?
column2: While Trent dogmatically anchored the priesthood to the Eucharistic sacrifice against Protestant denial, Orders is not merely a cultic altar-action (sacrificator). Holy Orders encompasses the whole tria munera (teaching, sanctifying, governing) and was instituted through an unfolding progression across Christ's public life, Pasch, and Pentecost.

column1: What are the four major scriptural stages in the dynamic institution of Holy Orders?
column2:
1. The Cenacle (Holy Thursday): Eucharistic-sacrificial mandate ("Hoc facite...", 1 Cor 11:24).
2. Easter Evening: Johannine commission & power to forgive sins (Jn 20:21–23).
3. Ascension: Universal missionary mandate and tria munera (Mt 28:18–20).
4. Pentecost: Descent of the Holy Spirit conferring interior drive, specific sacramental grace, and public launch (Acts 2).

column1: In John 20:21–23, how does the mission of the Apostles ("Sicut misit me Pater, et ego mitto vos") analogously reflect Christ's mission?
column2: Christ is the Missus a Patre substantially (His Person is the Word proceeding eternally from the Father); the Apostles are missi a Christo ministerially. Their authority is not their own, but depends on total fidelity as envoys bearing Christ's Spirit.

column1: In Acts 1:21–22, why was being a historical eyewitness to Jesus' ministry not sufficient for Matthias to be an Apostle?
column2: Historical companionship (material qualification) did not confer the apostolate. Matthias had to become a witness by receiving the divine election and the sacra potestas, showing that ministry requires an objective sacramental constitution beyond natural experience.

column1: What profound theological truth about sacramental ministry is revealed by comparing John 5:30 ("Non possum ego a meipso facere quicquam") and John 15:5 ("Sine me nihil potestis facere")?
column2: The metaphysics of the nihil posse: For themselves, the ministers can do nothing supernatural. This very incapacity unites them to Christ's mission, so that sacramental action is an act where man accomplishes by divine communication what he could never accomplish by natural power.

column1: How does Sacrosanctum Concilium 6 describe the relationship between the ministry of the Word and the celebration of the Sacraments?
column2: Word and Sacrament form an inadequately distinct binomial: Preaching proclaims redemption to awaken faith, while the Sacrament is the efficacious, transforming Word that actualises the salvation proclaimed.

column1: What role does Pentecost (Acts 2) play in the institution of Holy Orders (Lumen Gentium 19, Ad Gentes 4)?
column2: Pentecost is not a mere external ratification or assistance; it is a constitutive element that infuses the Holy Spirit as the interior missionary impulse (vis interna), confers specific sacramental grace, and inserts the apostolic ministry into the Trinitarian dynamic of salvation.

column1: In 2 Corinthians 5:20, why does Saint Paul describe the apostles as "ambassadors for Christ" (pro Christo legatione fungimur)?
column2: Because the Apostle acts with an authority that is not his own, but Christ's. He stands coram ecclesia (facing the community) in a dialogical relationship, proposing the divine gift that man must receive from Another (ab alio).

column1: Why can a Christian community never validly "democratically generate" or elect its own ministerial priest from below (a populo)?
column2: Because grace is heteronomous: no community can confer divine life upon itself, just as no one can baptise oneself. The ministerial priest acts in persona Christi Capitis, representing Christ the Head and Bridegroom confronting His Bride; authority flows downward (ab alto) through apostolic succession.

column1: According to Saint Paul (2 Cor 13:10; Eph 4:11–12; Rom 15:16), what is the finality of the sacra potestas given to the apostolic ministry in relation to the faithful?
column2: It is given ad aedificationem et non in destructionem (for building up, not destroying): its supreme finality is to serve the common priesthood of the faithful, so that the entire Body of Christ may become an acceptable, living offering sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

column1: How does the collegial dimension of the Twelve (Mark 3:14; CCC 877) reflect the Trinitarian life of God?
column2: The Twelve were chosen together and sent together as a permanent college under Peter. Their fraternal communion is not mere administrative teamwork, but a visible sacrament and reflection of the communion of the Divine Persons in the Holy Trinity.
